headline: HPE grows revenue 50% to a record $14.5 billion and raises its outlook, but the shares fall 16%
takeaway: Revenue jumped 50% with servers nearly doubling, earnings beat its own guidance and the outlook for fiscal 2027 went up. Yet gross margin fell 220 basis points from the previous quarter and the company warned of component shortages, and the shares dropped 16.3% to $40.19 the next day.
results: Revenue rose 50% to $14.5 billion. Non-GAAP gross margin was 38.2%, up 180 basis points from a year earlier but down 220 basis points from the previous quarter; non-GAAP operating margin rose to 16.9%. Diluted earnings per share were $1.26 GAAP and $1.43 non-GAAP, both above HPE’s own guidance ranges.

Cloud & AI revenue grew 68.6% to $11.3 billion, with servers up 94.7% to $8.8 billion and storage up 33.8%; the segment’s operating margin doubled to 18.4%. Networking, which includes the acquired Juniper business, grew 12.3% to $3.1 billion with a 22.1% margin. Free cash flow was $1.9 billion, and $979 million went back to shareholders.
mgmt: Chief executive Antonio Neri called fiscal 2026 a defining year, in which HPE built a new networking leader and expanded its role in AI infrastructure, and said the company now has greater earnings power. Chief financial officer Marie Myers said HPE raised its fiscal 2027 outlook for revenue, operating profit and free cash flow, and that free cash flow for the year was more than three times higher than in 2025.
According to news reports after the call, HPE warned that shortages of AI server components could extend into 2028, which weighed on the shares and on rivals such as Dell.
view: On the numbers, HPE delivered a strong quarter and a better outlook. The market reacted to two things: the sequential drop in gross margin, which suggests that more low-margin AI servers are diluting profitability, and the warning that component shortages could limit shipments for years. Combined with a broad sell-off in AI hardware on November 24, that produced a 16.3% fall.

At $40.19, HPE trades at about 13 times trailing earnings and roughly 7 times forward estimates, the cheapest valuation among large AI infrastructure suppliers. Part of the discount reflects its history of low growth and the debt taken on for Juniper; part reflects doubt that AI server margins can hold.

I think the sell-off overreacts. Networking gives HPE a higher-margin business than Dell or Super Micro, and the raised outlook shows demand is strong. The risk is that component shortages and pricing pressure keep margins down. At 7 times forward earnings, a lot of that is priced in.
watch: Gross margin in the next quarter, the effect of component shortages on shipments, and networking growth.
